children: President Donald Trump on Monday announced his administration's latest set of drug pricing deals, this time with the U.S. affiliate of Teva Pharmaceutical Industries and eight other midsize companies.

The White House said the agreements will give state Medicaid programs access to most-favored-nation pricing on drugs made by the companies-that is, pricing that matches rates paid in other countries where prices are typically lower than in the U.S.

"The agreements reduce prices on drugs that treat numerous costly, chronic, and even rare diseases, including hemophilia, Parkinson's disease, macular degeneration, glaucoma, liver disease, skin conditions, and various forms of cancer," according to a White House fact sheet.

A news release didn't list specific drugs or pricing terms by company, and the White House didn't immediately reply to a request for that information. The other eight companies that entered deals are BridgeBio, Astellas Pharma, Alcon, BeOne Medicines, CSL, Kyowa Kirin, Sun Pharma, and UCB.

On-shoring investments are part of the agreements, too. In total, the nine drug companies are "committed to invest at least $19.6 billion collectively in U.S. manufacturing in the near term," the White House said.
Teva shares briefly rose on news of the pricing deal, before ultimately losing 1% on Monday and closing the session at $36.05.

The stock fared worse last month, when it lost nearly 4% and landed at $30.15 the day after Trump threatened tariffs on generic drugs. Teva has long been known as a generic drug manufacturer, though the company's push to develop a branded drug portfolio has lately caught Wall Street's attention. Shares have gained 15.5% year to date.

When asked which medicines are subject to the deal, a Teva spokesperson told Barron's: "Conditions of the negotiation to reach a final agreement remain confidential; Teva remains in active discussions with the Trump Administration." The company said a final agreement on related Medicaid pricing would apply to "select medicines."
"The agreement also would include a prospective Most-Favored-Nation (MFN) commitment for applicable future innovative product launches," the spokesperson added.

Prior to Monday's event in the Oval Office, 17 major pharmaceutical companies had entered pricing agreements with the Trump administration, including Pfizer, Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk and most recently Regeneron in April.

While full terms of the deals haven't been disclosed, the agreements have generally included corporate commitments to lower certain drug prices and invest in American manufacturing operations, in exchange for relief from threatened tariffs on the pharmaceutical industry.
The Trump administration has touted the deals as an important step toward healthcare affordability, a big issue with voters heading into the midterm elections in November.
